topic: Front-desk exception escalation ladder for property managers
hook: If every exception lands in the same inbox, your front desk is still guessing.
captionInstagram:
What should an AI front desk escalate first for property managers?

Start with the exception paths that can create delay, compliance risk, or owner frustration if the workflow keeps acting like every message is routine. Good property management automation does not just answer faster. It knows when to route the next owner immediately.

That means missed-call text-back, leasing follow-up automation, maintenance intake automation, owner updates, vendor coordination, and property management CRM automation should all share a clear escalation ladder. Emergency maintenance, legal or fair-housing sensitive questions, approval thresholds, angry resident threads, duplicate records, and no-owner-found states should not sit in a general queue.

If your AI voice, SMS, and CRM workflows still dump every exception into manual cleanup, the team is not getting leverage. The system still lacks operating rules.

slides.title: If every exception lands in the same inbox,
slides.titleAccent: your front desk is still guessing.
slides.body: An AI front desk should not treat emergency maintenance, approval thresholds, angry residents, and broken CRM matches like routine conversations.

slides.title: Safety and habitability issues should jump the queue instantly.
slides.body: Leaks, no heat, no AC in extreme weather, electrical hazards, lockouts, flooding, and other emergency signals should route to the right human path immediately.
slides.footer: Goal: no emergency buried in general follow-up

slides.title: Sensitive leasing questions need a human review lane.
slides.body: Fair-housing risk, policy exceptions, complex concessions, or unclear unit fit should stop the automation from improvising beyond the approved playbook.
slides.footer: Goal: fast reply without unscripted risk

slides.title: Spend and policy limits should trigger the owner before work stalls.
slides.body: Maintenance scope, make-ready overages, vendor exceptions, and non-routine approvals should escalate with the summary, cost context, and next decision attached.
slides.footer: Goal: one summary, one approver, one next action

slides.title: Repeated or angry threads should not stay in drip logic.
slides.body: Multiple failed contacts, unresolved maintenance, or high-friction sentiment should move to a staffed lane before the relationship degrades further.
slides.footer: Goal: de-escalate before the next message goes out

slides.title: No match or duplicate match should pause write-back and route review.
slides.body: If the system cannot identify the right renter, owner, property, or work order cleanly, it should escalate instead of polluting the CRM with bad records.
slides.footer: Goal: protect the system of record

slides.title: Every workflow needs a named fallback owner.
slides.body: When no teammate, vendor, or owner path is obvious, the workflow should send the summary into a defined review queue with SLA and accountability.
slides.footer: Goal: no orphaned conversation, no hidden backlog
